title: Emergency Shelter
summary: How to select a safe location and build a basic survival shelter for protection.

sections.heading: Step 1 — Select a Safe Site
sections.body: Find a dry, flat area protected from the wind. Avoid low spots like ravines or dry riverbeds (risk of flash floods), the base of cliffs (falling rocks), or beneath dead trees (widowmakers). Ensure there is a plentiful supply of dry wood and foliage nearby.
sections.warning: Never build a shelter directly on a game trail, as animal encounters can occur.
sections.image_description: Shelter site located on a gentle slope surrounded by healthy trees

sections.heading: Step 2 — Construct a Support Frame
sections.body: Find a sturdy ridgepole (a long, thick log) and prop one end up in the fork of a tree or on a pair of crossed A-frame branches. Lean smaller support branches along both sides of the ridgepole at a 45-degree angle to form the rib structure of your shelter.
sections.warning: Ensure the frame is highly stable and can support weight before adding roofing materials.
sections.image_description: A long log resting in a tree fork with ribs leaned against it

sections.heading: Step 3 — Build a Ground Insulation Bed
sections.body: The ground will absorb your body heat rapidly. Build an insulation mattress by laying down a thick layer (at least 6-8 inches) of dry leaves, pine needles, ferns, or soft evergreen boughs inside the shelter. Sleep on top of this bed, not on bare earth.
sections.warning: Do not skip the insulation bed; it is more critical for warmth than the shelter walls.
sections.image_description: Thick bed of dry brown pine needles piled inside the shelter frame

sections.heading: Step 4 — Thatch and Cover the Outer Walls
sections.body: Place dense leafy branches, pine boughs, or strips of bark over the ribbed frame. Start from the bottom and work your way up to the top, overlapping layers like shingles on a house. This ensures that rainwater runs down the outer walls instead of dripping inside.
sections.warning: Leave a small opening for ventilation and entry on the side opposite the wind direction.
sections.image_description: Overlapping pine branches covering the outer frame like roof shingles

when_to_use: When stranded in the wilderness or during an emergency disaster where standard shelter is unavailable or unsafe.
do_not: Build in low-lying areas or narrow gorges
Use rotten or weak logs for the ridgepole frame
Burn a fire inside a closed, unventilated shelter space
